questions.question: Let $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)^{\top}\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the dot product. How does the orthogonal complement $W^\perp$ compare with the set complement $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus W$?
options: They are equal: both consist of all vectors outside $W$
$W^\perp$ is the $y$-axis; $(1,1)^{\top}$ lies in neither $W$ nor $W^\perp$
$W^\perp$ is the whole set $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus W$ plus $\boldsymbol{0}$
$\mathbb{R}^2\setminus W$ is a subspace, and $W^\perp$ is a smaller one

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product, let $W=\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{w}_1,\boldsymbol{w}_2\}$. Which test decides whether a vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ lies in $W^\perp$?

For a subset $W$ of a real inner-product space $V$, $W^\perp=\{\boldsymbol{v}\in V\colon\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0\text{ for all }\boldsymbol{w}\in W\}$. Let $W$ be a subspace. Why is $W\cap W^\perp=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$?
options: Because $W$ and $W^\perp$ are two different subspaces of $V$
A shared vector is orthogonal to itself, so it is $\boldsymbol{0}$
Because $\dim W+\dim W^\perp=\dim V$ leaves no room to overlap
Because $W^\perp$ is defined as the set complement $V\setminus W$

questions.question: For a subset $W$ of a real inner-product space $V$, $W^\perp=\{\boldsymbol{v}\in V\colon\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0\text{ for all }\boldsymbol{w}\in W\}$. In $V=\mathbb{R}^3$ with the dot product, what are $\{\boldsymbol{0}\}^\perp$ and $(\mathbb{R}^3)^\perp$?
Let $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)^{\top}\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the dot product. Which statement about subspaces $U$ with $\mathbb{R}^2=W\oplus U$ is correct?
options: There are many such $U$, and exactly one of them is $W^\perp$
There is exactly one such $U$, and it is $W^\perp$
Every such $U$ is orthogonal to $W$, so equals $W^\perp$
No such $U$ is orthogonal to $W$ unless $W=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product, what is $W^\perp$ for the line $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,-1)^{\top}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$?
The plane $W=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon 2x_1-x_2+3x_3=0\}$ carries the dot product. Which subspace is its orthogonal complement?
Let $W$ be a $3$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^7$ with the dot product. What is $\dim W^\perp$?
In $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product, let $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1,0)^{\top},(0,1,0,1)^{\top}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^4$. Which vector lies in $W^\perp$?

Consider nested subspaces $W_1=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0)^{\top}\}\subseteq W_2=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0)^{\top},(0,0,1)^{\top}\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ (dot product). Which vector is orthogonal to $W_1$ but not to all of $W_2$?

For a subset $W$ of a real inner-product space $V$, $W^\perp=\{\boldsymbol{v}\in V\colon\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0\text{ for all }\boldsymbol{w}\in W\}$. Why is $W^\perp$ a subspace of $V$ even when $W$ is not a subspace?
options: Because $W^\perp$ is only defined when $W$ is a subspace
It is not: for a non-subspace $W$ it is only an affine set
The defining conditions are linear and homogeneous in $\boldsymbol{v}$

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product, let $S=\{(1,0,0)^{\top},(0,1,0)^{\top}\}$, a set of two vectors that is not a subspace. What is $(S^\perp)^\perp$?

For a subset $W$ of a real inner-product space $V$, $W^\perp=\{\boldsymbol{v}\in V\colon\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0\text{ for all }\boldsymbol{w}\in W\}$. For subspaces $W_1,W_2$ of $V$, which set equals $(W_1+W_2)^\perp$?
In $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product, let $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,2,0)^{\top},(0,1,0,-1)^{\top}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^4$. Which set is a basis of $W^\perp$?

$W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^5$ (dot product) is spanned by three linearly independent vectors. A student lists three nonzero vectors $\boldsymbol{u}_1,\boldsymbol{u}_2,\boldsymbol{u}_3$, each orthogonal to $W$, as a basis of $W^\perp$. What must be true?
options: $\dim W^\perp=3$, so the list is a valid basis of $W^\perp$
$\dim W^\perp=2$, so the $\boldsymbol{u}_i$ are linearly dependent
$\dim W^\perp=5$, so two more vectors are needed
Some $\boldsymbol{u}_i$ must lie in $W$, as $W^\perp$ is too small

questions.question: For a subset $W$ of a real inner-product space $V$, $W^\perp=\{\boldsymbol{v}\in V\colon\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0\text{ for all }\boldsymbol{w}\in W\}$. In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the dot product, let $L=\{(x,y)\colon x=1\}$, a line not through $\boldsymbol{0}$. What is $L^\perp$?

$V$ is finite-dimensional with an inner product, $W$ is a subspace, and $U$ is a subspace with $V=W\oplus U$ and $\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0$ for all $\boldsymbol{u}\in U$, $\boldsymbol{w}\in W$. Must $U=W^\perp$?
options: No: $U$ is only one of many complements of $W$
No: it only follows that $U\subseteq W^\perp$
Yes: $U\subseteq W^\perp$ and their dimensions agree
Yes, but only if $U$ has an orthonormal basis

questions.question: Let $W_1$ and $W_2$ be subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^n$, with the dot product, such that $W_1^\perp=W_2^\perp$. What follows about $W_1$ and $W_2$?
options: Only $\dim W_1=\dim W_2$; the subspaces themselves may differ
Nothing: different subspaces can share one complement
$W_1\perp W_2$, since both are orthogonal to the same set

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product, let $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1,0)^{\top},(0,1,1,0)^{\top},(1,-1,0,0)^{\top}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^4$. What is $\dim W^\perp$?

On $\mathbb{R}^2$ use the inner product $\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}M\boldsymbol{y}=x_1y_1+2x_2y_2$ with $M=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$ instead of the dot product. With respect to it, what is $W^\perp$ for $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1)^{\top}\}$?
